2026-02-28.executive_summary: The single most important Canadian macro development this week was the Bank of Canada's decision to maintain its policy rate at 2.25%, signaling a cautious wait-and-see approach amid persistent inflation and moderating economic growth. Nationally, the BoC also issued, then revised, a compliance order for XTM Inc., temporarily ceasing then allowing recommencement of retail payment activities under supervision, highlighting the central bank's focus on financial sector oversight. Statistics Canada recently reported the national unemployment rate at 6.3% in the latest Labour Force Survey, indicating a cooling but still resilient labour market. In Alberta, a strong energy sector is driving projected provincial GDP growth of 2.8%, outperforming national averages. The proposed Roberts Bank Terminal 2 expansion in Metro Vancouver, valued at ~$3.5B, continues to be a critical infrastructure project to watch for trade capacity. Market conditions show crude oil (WTI) trading at $67.02 and gold at $5,230, reflecting global demand and geopolitical concerns, while the CAD faces pressure from a widening interest rate differential with the US. The key risk to watch in the week ahead is the upcoming US CPI report, which could significantly influence global rate expectations and the CAD.

national.analysis:
• Real GDP contracted annualized 0.6% in Q4 2025 (quarter-over-quarter), far below the −0.2% consensus, with manufacturing declining 1.5%; Q3 2025 had grown 0.6% (StatCan, February 27, 2026), setting full-year 2025 growth at 1.7%, the slowest since 2020. 1
  • Bank of Canada maintained the policy rate at 2.25% (Bank Rate 2.5%, deposit rate 2.20%) on January 28, 2026, with forward guidance signaling a pause through 2026 absent major shocks; markets assign 99% probability of no change at the next decision (March 18, 2026). 2
  • Labour force participation fell 0.4 percentage points to 65.0% in January 2026 (lowest since May 2021), while employment declined 25,000 month-over-month; full-time jobs gained 45,000 but part-time fell 70,000, signaling labour market softening amid economic headwinds. 3
  • Current account deficit narrowed sharply to $0.7 billion in Q4 2025 (seasonally adjusted), a $4.6 billion improvement from prior period, driven by exports rebounding 1.5% led by unwrought gold and aluminum shipments (StatCan, February 26, 2026). 4
  • Manufacturing and professional services showed deep sectoral divergence: manufacturing (NAICS 31–33) declined 2.7% month-over-month and 2.9% year-over-year, while professional services (NAICS 54) surged 3.1% monthly and fell 7.5% annually, signaling structural shifts and base effects (StatCan Table 36-10-0434-01). 5
  • Bank of Canada issued revised compliance orders to payment processor XTM Inc. on March 1, 2026, allowing limited retail payment activities under court-supervised Monitor following earlier enforcement action, highlighting fintech regulation amid digital payment sector stress. 6

2026-03-01.executive_summary: Canada's economy contracted sharply in Q4 2025, with annualized real GDP falling 0.6% against a −0.2% consensus forecast (StatCan, February 27, 2026), driven by a 1.5% manufacturing collapse offset partially by household spending and export gains led by unwrought gold and aluminum. The Bank of Canada held the policy rate steady at 2.25% on January 28, 2026, signaling a pause amid US tariff uncertainty and modest inflation at 2.3% year-over-year (January 2026). Ontario's unemployment spiked to 7.3% in January, highest among provinces, while Newfoundland and Labrador improved sharply with a −1.3 percentage-point monthly drop to 9.2%, reflecting divergent provincial labour markets. The current account deficit narrowed dramatically to $0.7 billion in Q4 2025, a $4.6 billion improvement, signaling trade rebalancing. Crude oil WTI at $72.08 and the CAD trading at 0.73 USD (up 5.6% year-over-year) reflect commodity volatility amid tariff escalation. Key risk: US tariffs imposed March 4, 2026 at 25% on most Canadian goods (10% on energy) threaten the 2026 growth projection of 1.1% and could trigger additional BoC rate cuts.

January manufacturing sales will indicate whether the 1.2% month-over-month gain in December 2025 manufacturing output persisted despite a 2.5% year-over-year contraction and ongoing tariff headwinds.
January retail sales data will assess consumer spending momentum following a 0.3% decline in food services and drinking places sales to $8.6 billion in December 2025.

Final January wholesale trade figures will confirm the advance estimate and reveal sector-specific inventory adjustments following fourth quarter 2025 inventory withdrawals that drove GDP contraction.

Federal Reserve policy decision will shape cross-border interest rate differentials and Canadian dollar valuation, currently at 0.73 USD (up 5.7% year-over-year), with implications for Bank of Canada rate path.
January GDP by industry will reveal whether the 0.2% expansion in December 2025, driven by services-producing industries, continued or whether tariff pressures accelerated manufacturing declines.

January payroll data will indicate whether the 35,400 job decline (down 0.2%) in December 2025 stabilized or worsened as businesses adjusted to fourth quarter inventory withdrawals and tariff uncertainty.

Following the March 3, 2026, announcement of $165.2 million for 22 Canadian critical minerals projects, project proponents will provide timelines and environmental assessments to unlock the $3.6 billion investment program.
Potential revisions to fourth quarter 2025 GDP data (currently showing 0.2% contraction) could alter Bank of Canada rate cut expectations, with markets pricing 40% odds of cuts by July 15, 2026.

Governor Tiff Macklem will update growth and inflation forecasts, clarifying whether the 2.25% overnight rate will be maintained or if cuts are warranted given fourth quarter 2025 GDP contraction and tariff impacts.
March employment data will reveal first-quarter labor market trends, critical for Bank of Canada policy as unemployment stood at 6.5% and payroll employment declined 0.2% in December 2025.
February building permits will assess whether housing starts can sustain the 238,049 annual rate amid elevated mortgage rates and Bank of Canada policy uncertainty.

Consultations launched February 27, 2026, by Minister François-Philippe Champagne will close, determining incentives for auto manufacturers amid tariff pressures that hit Quebec heavy truck production in November 2025.
March CPI data will confirm whether inflation remains near the 2.3% year-over-year target and assess whether tariff-related import costs are translating into broader consumer price pressures.

February manufacturing sales will indicate whether production declines in Quebec (down 0.3% in November) and the national 2.5% year-over-year manufacturing contraction are stabilizing or accelerating.
Governor Tiff Macklem will announce whether the 2.25% overnight rate will be maintained or cut, with markets pricing close to 40% probability of a cut by July 15, 2026, following weak Q4 2025 GDP.
February retail trade will reveal consumer spending trends after food services and drinking places sales declined 0.3% to $8.6 billion in December 2025 amid economic uncertainty.
February wholesale trade data will track inventory adjustments following fourth quarter 2025 business inventory withdrawals that drove the 0.2% GDP contraction.

watchlist.description: Following the March 3, 2026, announcement by Minister Mélanie Joly on 6G security and resilience at Mobile World Congress, Canada will release details on new Global Coalition on Telecommunications members and R&D investments.
February GDP by industry will determine whether the 0.2% expansion in December 2025 and the 0.3% contraction in Quebec's November output signal broader first quarter 2026 weakness.
February payroll data will confirm whether the 35,400 job decline (down 0.2%) in December 2025 reversed or persisted as tariff impacts and inventory adjustments flowed through the labor market.

April employment data will provide the first complete view of first quarter 2026 labor market conditions, critical for Bank of Canada rate decisions given December 2025 payroll declines and 6.5% unemployment.

Proponents of the Northern Road Link project will submit environmental assessments following open houses in Thunder Bay and Geraldton, advancing infrastructure to access the Ring of Fire's $22 billion economic potential.
